papers.title_in_file: Quantum Optimization for the Future Energy Grid: Summary and Quantum Utility Prospects
papers.version_note: The text is the arXiv v1 preprint of 26 Mar 2024 (12 pages), one copy only. The axis labels and legends inside Figs. 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 are garbled or missing in the text layer; their captions and the text around them were read.
papers.what_it_is: A project summary paper of the BMBF-funded Q-GRID project that reports benchmarks of classical, quantum-inspired and quantum-classical hybrid solvers on four energy grid optimization use cases (discount scheduling, community detection, prosumer coalition formation, Peer-2-Peer trading).

existing.note: The paper ties the crossover to the relative CO2 reduction metric of the discount scheduling problem (Section 2.2) and says what happens after it: Gurobi finds no converged result in the given time limit. The stored value does not name the metric or the problem.
existing.value: The authors report that, focusing on the relative CO2 reduction in the discount scheduling problem, a crossover in performance between Gurobi and Leap happens between 100 and 200 customers, after which Gurobi cannot find converged results in the given time limit, and note that the comparison is not directly fair because Gurobi is run on a local machine whilst the Leap hybrid solver is run on a proprietary D-Wave cloud architecture.
quotes: Focusing on the relative CO2 reduction, it is evident that a crossover in performance between Gurobi and Leap happens between 100 and 200 customers.
After that size, Gurobi cannot find converged results in the given time limit.
Although not a directly fair comparison since Gurobi is run on a local machine whilst the Leap hybrid solver is run on a proprietary D-Wave cloud architecture.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from Fig. 4 of a summary paper; the details are in the cited work.
existing.reader_inference: The size of the crossover is read by the authors from Fig. 4, whose axis text is lost in the text layer, so the numbers 100 and 200 are the authors' words only.

quotes: For select energy grid optimization problems, we demonstrate exponential classical optimizer runtime scaling even for small problem instances,
and present initial findings that variational quantum algorithms such as QAOA and hybrid quantum annealing solvers may provide more favourable runtime scaling to obtain similar solution quality.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the body supports it with Gurobi runtimes (Fig. 5) and exact-solver runtimes against 1-round QAOA (Fig. 7).
existing.reader_inference: The runtime scaling for hybrid quantum annealing (Leap) is not shown as a runtime curve in the text; the body claim of favourable scaling is made for 1-round QAOA in Section 4.2.

quotes: We have demonstrated that quantum optimization approaches may provide some advantages over traditional classical optimization approaches in terms of application-specific benchmarks or hybrid algorithm solution quality,
however further investigation is needed to explore any evidence of potential quantum utility in the energy sector.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in their conclusion (Section 6).

assertions.value: The authors state that Q-GRID is a 3-year project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), awarded in 2021 as part of a call for application networks for quantum computing.
quotes: The ”Q-GRID” project is a 3-year funded project by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) awarded as part of the “Anwendungsnetzwerk fu¨r das Quantencomputing” call in 2021.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its project scope (Section 1).

assertions.value: The authors state that the project goal is to investigate the basic applicability of quantum computing optimization techniques in the energy sector and, because of NISQ computers, to identify the current major problem-specific challenges before fault-tolerant quantum computers are developed and deployed.
quotes: The project’s goal is to investigate the basic applicability of quantum computing optimization techniques in the energy sector and, due to Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) computers, identify the current major
problem-specific challenges before practical development and deployment of fault-tolerant quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its aim and scope (Section 1).

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper outlines four proposed approaches for sub-problems of two overarching use cases, load scheduling using dynamic pricing and virtual community and microgrid creation, and describes each by background, mathematical formulation and benchmarking results.
quotes: In this project summary paper, we outline four proposed approaches for sub-problems related to the above overarching use-cases.
We will describe them in terms of their background, mathematical formulation, and benchmarking results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope (Section 1).
assertions.reader_inference: The four approaches are discount scheduling (Section 2), community detection (Section 3), prosumer coalition formation (Section 4) and Peer-2-Peer trading (Section 5).

assertions.value: The authors state that current workflows in finding applied quantum computing use cases typically involve small-scale toy models, where researchers balance problem complexity against qubit usage because of limited resources.
quotes: Current workflows in finding applied quantum computing use-cases typically involve small-scale toy models where researchers attempt to find the right balance between problem complexity and qubit usage due to limited resources.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the field, given without citation or evidence.

assertions.value: The authors define the Discount Scheduling Problem (DSP) as finding personalized price patterns for each customer to optimize load distribution, with the main goal of lowering the overall CO2 emissions of all customers by shifting load to times when the grid CO2 intensity is small.
quotes: Therefore, we aim to find personalized price patterns for each customer to optimize load distribution. We refer to this as Discount Scheduling Problem (DSP).
We choose the main goal of the optimization problem to be lowering the overall CO2 emissions of all customers by shifting the load to times when the grid CO2 intensity It is small
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the DSP and its main goal itself (Section 2 and 2.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that the central assumption of the DSP formulation is that a given discount or penalty influences the customer's behavior so that consumption changes proportionally.
quotes: The central assumption of the formulation is that a given discount (or penalty) influences the customer’s behavior to alter their consumption proportionally.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the assumption of its own formulation (Section 2.1).
assertions.reader_inference: The result of the benchmark depends on this assumption; no test of it against real customer behavior is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the DSP objective is subject to several constraints, such as customers not changing their total consumed energy over the optimization horizon and the momentary change in consumption of all customers being bounded to preserve system stability, and they refer the reader to earlier work for the constraints and the decomposition method.
quotes: This objective function is subject to several constraints such as not wanting customers to change their total consumed energy over the optimization horizon, and, enforcing the momentary change in consumption of all customers to be bounded, to preserve system stability.
We refer the reader to [4] for further details on the mathematical structure of the constraints and of the decomposition method.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its problem constraints (Section 2.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that the integer binary encoding of the discounts is space efficient, allowing an exponential number of categories to be represented with a linearly growing number of qubits.
quotes: This encoding is space efficient, allowing for an exponential number of categories to be represented with a linearly growing number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper gives the encoding (Eqs. 1 and 2) but no separate derivation of the claim.
assertions.reader_inference: The number of binary variables per discount is given as Q = floor(log2 Nk + 1), which is consistent with a logarithmic number of qubits per discount; the count of qubits for the whole problem also grows with customers and time steps.

assertions.value: The authors state that the DSP is judged on several metrics at the same time: the CO2 reduction as the main metric, the energy (the objective, being the rescaled CO2 reduction with the penalties added), and the average relative cost savings, which show how evenly discounts are distributed across customers.
quotes: CO2 reduction: First and foremost, the CO2 reduction is the central goal of the DSP, hence it is also the main metric that is investigated.
Energy: The energy, or objective, of the optimization problem consists of the rescaled CO2 reduction with the penalties added.
Average relative cost savings: How evenly distributed are the discounts across all customers?
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own metrics (Section 2.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that they used Gurobi as the state-of-the-art purely classical baseline and compared it with D-Wave's LeapHybridCQM solver (Leap) and with their own problem-specific decomposition routine, called Decomp-Gurobi, Decomp-Leap or Decomp-QPU depending on the solver used for the chunk problems.
quotes: As a state-of-the-art purely classical baseline, we used Gurobi1 [5]. This was compared to D-Wave’s LeapHybridCQM solver [6]
These two out-of-the-box solvers are compared against our own problem-specific decomposition routine [4], subsequently called Decomp-Gurobi, Decomp-Leap or Decomp-QPU
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark setup (Section 2.2).
assertions.reader_inference: Only Gurobi, Leap, Decomp-Gurobi[50] and Decomp-Leap[50] appear in the legends of Figs. 1 to 4; no Decomp-QPU result is reported in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that all experiments with Gurobi were conducted on an M1 MacBook Pro (2020) with Gurobi version 9.0.
quotes: All experiments with Gurobi were conducted on an M1 MacBook Pro (2020) with Gurobi Version 9.0
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup (footnote 1).
assertions.reader_inference: The footnote is attached to the Section 2 experiments; the same Gurobi runs for Sections 3 and 5 are not described with hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that they set the customer price elasticity to one for all customers (turning its effect off) and use five discount categories with a 50% discount at most, so that a discount of 50% would result in an increase in the customer's consumption by 50%.
quotes: we turn their effect off and set them all to one. Next, we use five discount categories, with a 50% discount maximally.
As a consequence, a discount of, e.g., 50% would result in an increase in the customer’s consumption by 50%.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark parameters (Section 2.2).
assertions.reader_inference: With the elasticity set to one for every customer, the benchmark does not test customer heterogeneity, which the formulation was written to allow.

assertions.value: The authors report that for a 100-customer example, analysed with four solvers (Gurobi, Leap, and two m = 50 decomposition methods using the same solvers as the subroutine), the particular discount matrices differ significantly from one another while the effective overall energy result stays similar regarding the CO2 reduction.
quotes: Let us first examine the optimization result of the different solvers in detail for a 100-customer example
We analyze the solutions of four solvers, Gurobi, Leap, and two m = 50 decomposition methods with the same solvers as the subroutine.
Although the particular solutions differ significantly from one another, the effective overall energy result stays similar (essentially the same), regarding the CO2 reduction.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one 100-customer instance.

assertions.value: The authors report that Gurobi provides a more greedy discount allocation by giving discounts to relatively few customers, while Leap distributes similar discounts to all customers, and state that they do not optimize for this fairness-style metric.
quotes: Gurobi provides a more greedy discount allocation approach by providing discounts to relatively few customers.
On the other hand, Leap distributes similar discounts to all customers.
Remember: We do not optimize for this metric.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical decomposition routine greatly outperforms the general-purpose solvers and that, at the higher customer sizes, the decomposition method with Leap as subsolver remains competitive.
quotes: Nevertheless, the classical decomposition routine greatly outperforms the general-purpose solvers, and in the higher customer size problem sizes, the decomposition method with Leap as subsolver remains competitive.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from Fig. 4.
assertions.reader_inference: The best performer in the DSP benchmark is a classical decomposition method, so the DSP result does not show the quantum component beating the best classical method.

assertions.value: The authors state that Leap is a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm with the benefit of solving larger problems than possible directly on current quantum hardware while also supporting more sophisticated optimization models that include hard constraints.
quotes: This has the benefit of solving larger problems than possible directly on current quantum hardware while also supporting more sophisticated optimization models that include hard constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author description of a vendor product, with no evidence in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that Community Detection is a well-known NP-hard problem with many use cases.
quotes: Our approach is built on Community Detection, a well-known NP-hard problem with many use cases [7].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that augmenting the community detection cost function with additional constraints makes the problem substantially harder classically at smaller instance sizes, which they describe as a prerequisite for well formulated near-term quantum utility applications.
quotes: which as we will show, make the problem substantially harder classically at smaller instance sizes - a prerequisite for well formulated near-term quantum utility applications
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper supports the first part with one Gurobi runtime figure (Fig. 5) and cites another work for the prerequisite.

assertions.value: The authors state that, inspired by the GCS-Q algorithm, they apply a divisive greedy heuristic that finds the best community structure with K = 2, splits the network in two, and repeats this recursively in the two sub-nets until the solution quality cannot be further improved.
quotes: we apply a divisive algorithm (a greedy heuristic) that tries to find the best community structure with K = 2, i.e., splitting the network in two.
This is recursively repeated in the two sub-nets until the solution quality cannot be further improved.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own algorithm (Section 3.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that, as a peculiarity of their approach, they dynamically compute the weights of the adjacency matrix from the current load and production in the grid, using the power flowing through a line as the weight.
quotes: we dynamically compute the weights of the adjacency matrix based on the current load and production in the grid
use the power that flows through a specific line as the weight in
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own graph weighting (Section 3.1).

assertions.value: The authors report that Gurobi's time to solution on the single-problem community detection formulation, run until convergence, shows the exponential nature of the problem, and that the problem becomes harder with self-reliance; the fit labels in Fig. 5 read 1.13N without self-reliance and 1.42N with self-reliance, with the exponent N printed flat in the text layer.
quotes: Figure 5 demonstrates the exponential runtime nature of the problem.
Here, Gurobi is run until convergence for self-reliance turned on or off, clearly showing that the problem becomes harder with self-reliance.
Without self-reliance Fit: 1.13N
With self-reliance Fit: 1.42N
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The fit labels most likely read 1.13 to the power N and 1.42 to the power N, an exponential growth rate in the number of nodes; the node range in Fig. 5 is roughly 10 to 40, so the fit covers small instances only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark grid instances are IEEE power system test cases provided by pandapower, adapted to behave more like residential power grids, with consumption and production sampled randomly from two shifted normal distributions, and with 50% of the actors producers and 50% consumers.
quotes: The benchmarking grid instances comprise of IEEE power system test cases provided by pandapower [17] and have been adapted to behave more like residential power grids.

The consumption and production data is sampled randomly from two shifted normal distributions (one for production and one for consumption). 50% of the actors are producers and the other 50% are consumers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark setup (Section 3.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that for each test case they sample five data instances, set the self-reliance penalty to 0.1 after preliminary trials, estimate the number of communities K with the Louvain algorithm (median over runs), and run each solver five times per instance, giving 25 runs per case; the single-problem timeout is 6 s and each QUBO solution in the Divisive runs is given 3 s.
quotes: we sample five data instances. The self-reliance penalty λ is set to 0.1 due to preliminary trials which demonstrated the best trade-off with this setting.
the number of communities K is estimated using Louvain’s algorithm, by running the heuristic and then choosing the median number of communities which were found.

Each solver is run five times for a single instance, resulting in 25 runs for one case. In the single-problem runs, the timeout is fixed to 6 s. In the Divisive runs, each QUBO solution is given 3 s timeout
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark setup (Section 3.2).
assertions.reader_inference: The short timeouts (6 s and 3 s) limit what a Gurobi comparison can show; the solution-quality curves in Fig. 6 are normalized to the best-found energy, not to a proven optimum.

assertions.value: The authors report that the divisive approach delivers good results over almost all solvers except for QA, which loses solution quality immediately; that on the first split for the larger instances Leap is the best performer, followed by SA, Gurobi, and QSA; and that, except for the smaller cases, one of the Leap approaches always slightly outperforms Louvain.
quotes: The divisive approach delivers good results over almost all solvers, except for QA, which loses solution quality immediately.
rendering Leap as the best performer, followed by SA, Gurobi, and QSA.
Except for the smaller cases, one of the Leap approaches always slightly outperforms Louvain.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from Fig. 6.
assertions.reader_inference: QA is not defined in the solver list of Section 3.2; the legend of Fig. 6a shows DW, so QA most likely means the D-Wave QPU. Leap beats Louvain only slightly and by a quality margin the text gives no number for.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing earlier work, that with n agents there are a staggering number of possible partitions of order n to the power n, and that the only algorithm capable of finding an optimal solution within reasonable computational complexity is dynamic programming, which does so in time of order 3 to the power n.
quotes: leading to a staggering O(nn) possible partitions.
Dynamic Programming algorithm, achieving this in O(3n) time [24].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work; the exponents are printed flat in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The flat strings O(nn) and O(3n) are read as O(n^n) and O(3^n).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that transforming the coalition problem to an Induced Subgraph Game allows it to be recast as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem, but that the problem remains NP-complete.
quotes: The transformation of to ISG allows the problem to be recast as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, enabling more computationally efficient approaches. However, it is important to note that the problem remains NP-complete [22].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the value function nonlinearities in v(Cl) mean the ISG framework is not directly applicable to their CSG, so they use an ISG with pairwise joint utilities that approximate the GSCP, with the weights found by a quadratic programming problem that minimizes the mean squared error between the value functions of the GSCP and the approximate ISG.
quotes: The value function nonlinearities in v(Cl) mean this framework is not directly applicable to our CSG.
However, we can make use of an ISG based on pairwise joint utilities w˜ij which approximate our GSCP.
pairwise weights that minimize the mean squared error between the value functions of the GSCP and an approximate ISG
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own approximation (Section 4.1, Eq. 8).
assertions.reader_inference: The benchmark in Section 4.2 therefore tests QAOA on an approximate game, not on the exact coalition value function; GSCP is not defined in the text (probably a typo for CSG).

assertions.value: The authors state that they benchmark an exact classical solver against 1-round QAOA to find optimal bipartitions; solution quality is the ratio between the value of the optimized coalition obtained by 1-round QAOA and that of the exact classical solver; results are averages across 20 problem instances; the number of shots across all prosumer counts is fixed to 212 as printed in the text layer.
quotes: we elaborate on our benchmark between an exact classical solver and 1-round QAOA to find optimal bipartitions through iterative minimization of Eq. (9).
The solution quality is determined by calculating the ratio between the value of the optimized coalition obtained by 1-round QAOA and that achieved by the exact classical solver.
Results for each number of prosumers showcase an average across 20 problem instances.
the number of shots across all prosumer counts is fixed to 212
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark setup (Section 4.2).
assertions.reader_inference: The 212 is probably 2 to the power 12 (4096 shots) with the exponent flattened. The text does not say whether QAOA ran on hardware or a simulator, so the QAOA runtime in Fig. 7 may be a simulated runtime.

assertions.value: The authors report, for an average across 20 realizations for the case of 18 prosumers, that the graphs from the CSG to ISG mapping are nearly fully connected across all system sizes, and that the weight distribution has both positive and negative values and forms a Gaussian distribution centered close to zero.
quotes: The weight distribution showcases an average across 20 realizations for the case of 18 prosumers.
Our observations reveal that the graphs generated from transferring CSG to ISG are nearly fully connected across all system sizes.
the weight distribution exhibits a comprehensive range, incorporating both positive and negative values, thereby forming a Gaussian distribution centered close to zero.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the exact classical solver shows a noticeable increase in runtime that becomes impractical beyond 30 prosumers, while 1-round QAOA, which does not guarantee an exact solution, shows a more favorable scaling in running time; they state that the results demonstrate a potential competitive advantage for quantum-based solvers in problem size scaling to runtime while maintaining a high solution quality.
quotes: The exact classical solver, due to its computational complexity, experiences a noticeable increase in runtime that becomes impractical beyond 30 prosumers.
while 1-round QAOA does not guarantee an exact solution, it demonstrates a more favorable scaling in terms of running time
These results demonstrate a potential competitive advantage for quantum-based solvers compared to exact solvers in terms of problem size scaling to runtime while maintaining a high solution quality.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from Fig. 7; the solution-quality values are in the figure and not in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against an exact solver on an approximate game, with a fixed shot count and 1-round QAOA; no comparison with a classical heuristic such as the divisive method is given, so the result does not show an advantage over the best classical method.

assertions.value: The authors propose a Peer-2-Peer auction formulation that matches grid participants so that the resulting logical power flow is as close to the actual physical power flow in the grid as possible, with the objective of minimizing the mismatch between physical and logical power flow.
quotes: We propose a problem formulation matching the grid participants in a Peer-2-Peer auction so that the resulting logical power flow is as close to the actual physical power flow in the grid as possible.
Finally, we can formulate the objective function as the minimization of the mismatch between physical and logical power flow:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own formulation (Section 5.1, Eq. 16).

assertions.value: The authors state that a significant drawback of the earlier matching approach is that the physical power flow in the grid is not respected, which can disadvantage producers closer to their potential consumers by letting producers further away in the grid undercut them.
quotes: A significant drawback of this matching approach is that the physical power flow in the grid is not respected.

This mismatch of the logical power flow to the physical power flow can result in an unfair disadvantage for producers closer to their potential consumers being undercut by producers further away in the grid.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about earlier work, without a measurement in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluate the formulation on benchmark grids from the pandapower library, the largest having 39 prosumers, with Gurobi, Simulated Annealing (SA) and Tabu Search with Simulated Annealing on sub-problems (QSA); SA and QSA use 1000 reads, and each case and solver is run 10 times with a maximum run time of 30 seconds.
quotes: The largest grid evaluated consisting of 39 prosumers is visualized in Fig. 9.
Tabu Search with Simulated Annealing on sub-problems (QSA)
The SA and QSA solvers are executed with the number of reads set to 1000. We run the optimization 10 times for each case and solver with a maximum run time of 30 seconds.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its benchmark setup (Section 5.2).
assertions.reader_inference: SA and QSA run classically here (the paper itself calls them quantum-inspired), so this benchmark involves no quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that the differences in solution quality between the examined solvers are marginal, in that Gurobi no longer gives significantly better objective values than the quantum-inspired solvers SA and QSA, and that the power flow formulation exhibits a far smaller powerflow mismatch than the optimal solution of the earlier non-PF formulation; they state that the PF formulation is harder to solve classically and that the quantum-inspired heuristics deliver satisfactory results.
quotes: for the examined solvers are marginal, i.e., we no longer obtain significantly better objective values with Gurobi as we do with the quantum-inspired solvers SA and QSA.
As expected, compared to the optimal solution of the non-PF formulation given in [28], the PF formulation exhibits a far smaller powerflow mismatch.
The PF formulation is harder to solve classically, and the quantum-inspired heuristics deliver satisfactory results.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from Fig. 8; no numbers are given in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: SA and QSA are classical, so the result shows classical heuristics matching Gurobi, not a quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results demonstrate that matching a grid's participants on the physical power flow can significantly increase the fairness of the matched prosumers regarding how the power flows in the grid.
quotes: These results demonstrate that matching a grid’s participants based on the physical power flow in the grid can significantly increase the fairness of the matched prosumers regarding how the power flows in the grid.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; fairness is measured only as the power flow mismatch (Eq. 16).

assertions.value: The authors state that in their current formulation the energy price is not respected, possibly resulting in consumers overpaying for the energy they consume, and that a solution could be to extend the formulation with a price matching.
quotes: However, in our current formulation, the energy price is not respected, possibly resulting in consumers overpaying for the energy they consume.
to extend our proposed formulation with a price matching similar to the one suggested in [28].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own formulation (Section 5.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that their initial results suggest quantum computing may be a key enabling technology in the future energy transition, insofar as it may be able to solve business problems which are already challenging at small problem instance sizes.
quotes: These initial results suggest that quantum computing may be a key enabling technology in the future energy transition insofar that they may be able to solve business problems which are already challenging at small problem instance sizes.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim, hedged with may, resting on initial results.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion (Section 6) is more careful than this sentence: it says further investigation is needed on any evidence of potential quantum utility.

assertions.value: The authors state that they outlined 4 industry-related use cases for applied quantum optimization to the energy sector and benchmarked the performance of the quantum algorithms versus classical counterparts in each use case.
quotes: we have outlined 4 industry-related use-cases for applied quantum optimization to the energy sector.
In each of the use-cases, we have benchmarked the performance of the quantum algorithms versus classical counterparts.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author summary of the paper's own work.
assertions.reader_inference: In Section 5 only classical and quantum-inspired solvers (Gurobi, SA, QSA) are benchmarked, so the claim of quantum algorithms in each use case holds only if quantum-inspired heuristics count.
